**Step 1, the smallest check that closes it.** The missing check is the one the random test has and the checking testbench lacks: a model of the queue, and a comparison of every popped word with the model's oldest. It is written as a module bound to the FIFO beside the temporal-properties chapter's checker, which is read by path and not edited. It judges pushes and pops by the contract at the ports, as that checker does:

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch25-mutation-testing/fifth-tb/fifo_data_sva.sv" lines="22-37"}
```

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch25-mutation-testing/fifth-tb/fifo_data_bind.sv"}
```

The traffic is the checking testbench's own, unchanged. The data check reads no internal signal, so a kill it makes is a kill at the ports, not one of the white-box kills of @sec-ch25-equiv. Its formal counterpart is the tracked-word check of @sec-ch19-track, which follows one arbitrary word instead of all of them.

**Step 2, the control.** A check that cannot fail closes nothing. The fifth testbench, the checking testbench with the data check bound beside its checker, must pass the repaired FIFO and fail the original of @sec-ch01-example, as the control runs of @sec-ch21-example did for that chapter's bound:

```{.text include="examples/ch25-mutation-testing/fifth-tb/run.out" lines="1-6"}
```

**Step 3, the mutants again.** The 44 source mutants as a schema, at the simulator's default initial values and with randomized ones under seeds 1 to 5, and the uniform sample of 1,000 netlist mutations of @sec-ch25-sampling:

```{.text include="examples/ch25-mutation-testing/fifth-tb/run.out" lines="7-22"}
```

**Step 4, reading the new matrix.** All fifteen data-path mutants now die, and nothing else changes. `m35` was already killed, because the checking testbench's traffic drains the FIFO. The three reset deletions `m09`, `m11` and `m13` still survive at default initial values and die with randomized ones; the data check sees `m09` and `m11` once their pointers start somewhere other than zero. The four equivalent mutants survive, as they must, and `m44` is still killed by `Sync_A`. On the netlist sample the kill rate rises from 39 to 899 of 1,000, level with the random test's 896 within any interval. @tbl-ch25-report is the before and after.

{{< include /examples/ch25-mutation-testing/fifth-tb/tbl-ch25-report.md >}}

**Step 5, the sentence.** The result is written with everything that qualifies it, and with the white-box kill apart, as @sec-ch25-equiv asked. The example counts the kills at the ports by running the fifth testbench once more with `Sync_A` made vacuous, the checker's count input tied to its own occupancy counter, on the source mutants and on the netlist sample:

```{.text include="examples/ch25-mutation-testing/fifth-tb/run.out" lines="23-31"}
```

On the repaired FIFO, the checking testbench with the data check kills, at the ports, 36 of the 44 source mutants of this chapter's operator set at the simulator's default initial values and 39 of 44 with randomized initial values under five seeds; the white-box `Sync_A` adds one more, `m44`, a mutant the miter proves equivalent. Of the 39 mutants outside the five equivalent ones, that is a score of 36 of 39 at default values and 39 of 39 with randomized ones; the five survivors at the ports are the five equivalent mutants, one of them equivalent only under the formal tool's reset model; it kills 899 of a uniform sample of 1,000 of the 9,281 netlist mutations Yosys 0.68 makes of the file, all of them at the ports, interval 0.879 to 0.917; and the equivalent fraction of that population is 0.060, interval 0.022 to 0.126, from a formal sample of 100. Coverage goes beside it, unchanged by the new check, because the stimulus is unchanged.

"Closes the gap" means the data-path gap. It does not mean a perfect score. Three of the remaining seven survivors at default initial values are real bugs, missing resets, that this testbench catches only when the simulator's initial values are randomized, and the step that closes that gap is a change to how the regression runs, not to the testbench.

The netlist sample has survivors too, about one in ten of the thousand, and the formal sample of @sec-ch25-sampling says what to expect among them: some equivalent mutations, which nothing can kill, and deep mutations of the memory that a longer or differently shaped run would reach. The next step would be to classify the survivors of this sample with the miter, not to add checks until the number moves. The report also has a home beyond this chapter. The seeds, plusargs and initial-value modes that the result depends on are inputs of the build, which belong to Reproducible Verification, and a kill rate beside coverage in a sign-off table, with the same qualifiers this section wrote into its sentence, belongs to Metrics, Closure and Sign-off.

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example"}
Qualifying a testbench in six steps. (1) Control: show that the testbench passes the design and fails a known-bad version of it. (2) Mutate under a stated fault model, at every site, or as a uniform sample of a stated size from the complete list. (3) Run the mutants as a schema, with randomized initial values and recorded seeds, and with a checkless testbench beside the real ones as the control that exposes kills made by the harness. (4) Classify the survivors with a miter that compares what the contract specifies: equivalent outright, under an invariant, or under a tool's model; or not equivalent, and then a stimulus gap or a checking gap. (5) Fix the gap the survivors name, not the score. (6) Report kill rate, equivalent fraction and score, each with its interval, its $n$ and its seeds, with the fault model, beside coverage.
:::

## Future directions {#sec-ch25-future}

::: {.callout-important title="Future Directions"}
Large language models now appear on both sides of mutation testing, and the results so far are measured on software, or reported in preprints, and none is compared with a formal miter. As *generators*, Foster and colleagues, industrial authors at Meta, report a system that writes mutants aimed at a stated concern, privacy, and then tests that kill them: over 10,795 Kotlin classes it produced 9,095 mutants and 571 tests, of which engineers accepted 73% [@foster2025ach]. For RTL, the BugGen preprint uses a pipeline of language-model agents to insert functional bugs into five OpenTitan IP blocks, 500 bugs at 17.7 validated bugs per hour [@jasper2025buggen]. As *classifiers* of equivalence, Tian and colleagues report that language-model techniques improved F1 by 35.69% on average over earlier techniques on 3,302 pairs of Java mutants [@tian2024llmequiv], and Foster and colleagues' equivalence detector reached a precision of 0.79 and a recall of 0.47, rising to 0.95 and 0.96 with pre-processing their abstract does not describe [@foster2025ach]. And as an *audit*, the single-author GateTruth preprint uses mutation kill rate to judge the testbenches of an LLM RTL benchmark, and reports that 72% of 46 auditable RTLLM v2.0 designs fall below a 95% kill threshold [@bhadra2026gatetruth]: the coverage testbench's zero of @sec-ch25-motivation, found in a benchmark. For finite-state hardware a miter is the exact classifier whenever its proof finishes, so an LLM's equivalence verdicts can be scored against ground truth on populations like this chapter's; that experiment belongs to Machine Learning in Verification and to @sec-ch34, whose @sec-ch34-evaluation already names mutation kill rate as the hidden metric that a generated testbench should be judged by. Three further directions stay open here. Higher-order mutants, several changes at once, are where the coupling effect would be tested on hardware. The DMA of @sec-ch11, with its protocol properties, is the natural next population, with a richer state space and a bus contract to compare in its miter. And Safety and Security Verification asks the same question of the silicon instead of the testbench, through fault injection.
:::

## Summary {#sec-ch25-summary}

- Kill rate and coverage are different axes. On the repaired FIFO, the coverage testbench reaches every line, branch and expression point and kills none of 44 mutants, and the random test, with the same line, branch and expression coverage, kills 35. Coverage cannot tell a testbench with a checker from one without.
- A kill needs four things: reach the mutated point, infect the state, propagate to a port, and reveal through a check. Code coverage measures part of the first, and nothing in a coverage report measures the other three.
- An operator set applied at every site is a fault model, and a kill rate means nothing without it. The FIFO's ten operators make 44 mutants; lint kills seven before any simulation; mutants of one comparison are not independent evidence.
- A survivor is a stimulus gap, a checking gap, an artifact of a tool's model, or an equivalent mutant, and the matrix alone cannot say which. The checking testbench's fifteen data-path survivors are a checking gap; the random test's `m35` is a stimulus gap of one seed.
- Equivalence is what the miter compares, and only an unbounded proof establishes it. The FIFO's five equivalent mutants are of three kinds: outright (`m32`, `m36`), under a reachable-state invariant (`m43`, and `m44`, whose invariant relates the two copies' counts), and only under the formal tool's reset model (`m05`), which applies reset at the start of a trace and never again. A white-box assertion such as `Sync_A` can kill a mutant that is equivalent at the ports; report such kills apart.
- The simulator's initial values are part of the oracle: three missing resets survive every testbench at the default and die when initial values are randomized.
- The formal property set kills every non-equivalent source mutant it can read; on the netlist its fourteen misses are bounds of the search, not gaps in the specification, and simulation's deep traces kill them.
- The fault model sets the score: the checking testbench kills half the source mutants and under four percent of the netlist mutations, about three quarters of which lie on the memory's lines.
- Sample uniformly from the complete list, and report kill rate, equivalent fraction and score separately, each with its interval: on the netlist, 0.060 equivalent [0.022, 0.126] and a random-test score of 93 of 94. Plugging the ends of two separately computed intervals into a ratio ignores the relation between the quantities, here that an equivalent mutant is never killed, and can give a "score" above one.
- The software evidence licenses the method, not its numbers: mutants couple to most real faults, a score's correlation with fault detection is mostly suite size, and high scores matter most.
- A harness that kills by itself, or a seed sweep that runs one seed, is the first thing to rule out, and a checkless testbench is the control that finds it.

## Exercises {#sec-ch25-exercises}

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise"}
1. A uniform sample of 100 netlist mutations is run, and the directed test kills 30. Give the two-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson interval for its kill rate, and say whether it contains the population rate of 2,725 kills in 9,281.
2. A formal sample of 100 mutations finds 6 equivalent. Give the two-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson interval for the equivalent fraction.
3. The random test's population kill rate is 0.8905, and the equivalent fraction is estimated at 0.060 with interval [0.022, 0.126]. Compute $k/(1-e)$ at $e = 0.060$ and at both ends of the interval. The value at the upper end is above one. Is the division wrong, or one of its inputs? Use the fact that an equivalent mutant is never killed.
4. For a sample of 1,000 mutants and the worst case $p = 0.5$, give the half-width of a 95% interval for the kill rate by Chebyshev's inequality and by the normal approximation.
5. Two of the FIFO's equivalent mutants are equivalent outright, `m32` and `m36`. Synthesis with one Yosys script finds only one of them identical to the original. Which, and why not the other?
6. Why can this tool's bounded search, which knows no completeness threshold, never report `m43` equivalent? k-induction proves the flag half of `m43`'s miter with no helper invariant, but not the whole miter even with `count <= 16` assumed on both copies. What does the comparison of `rd_data` need that the flags do not?
7. Under `m44`, starting from reset, apply five pushes and then two pops, one operation per cycle. What value does the mutant's `count` hold, and what are `full` and `empty`? What does the repaired FIFO show at the ports?
8. Is `m44` killed under weak mutation, comparing the state immediately after the mutated statement executes? If so, after how many accepted operations from reset?
9. A colleague's miter compares `full` and `empty` and leaves `rd_data` out. Name three source mutants it would call equivalent that the chapter's miter refutes, and say which class of survivor of @sec-ch25-survivors that comparison would excuse as a whole.
10. The testbench `tb_async_reset.sv` pushes three words, pulses `rst_n` between two clock edges and checks `empty` before the next edge, and it kills `m05`. Which of the six other mutants that every book testbench leaves alive at default initial values, `m09`, `m11`, `m13`, `m32`, `m36` and `m43`, does it kill as well, and is the timing of the pulse the reason?
11. The random test kills `m35` under 53 of 100 seeds. If each seed killed it independently with probability 0.53, how many seeds would give a 99% chance of at least one kill? Why might the kills under different seeds not be independent events with one probability?
12. The coverage testbench killed 0 of 1,000 sampled netlist mutations. Give the exact one-sided 95% upper bound on its kill rate, by the formula of @sec-ch21-clean (not the two-sided end the run prints), and say why the bound, though correct, says nothing about whether this testbench could ever kill a mutant.
:::
